questions.problem: A shipping company’s management noted that the growth of a ship’s speed is directly proportional to the difference between the ship’s maximum cruising speed and its current speed. Let $V(t)$ be the speed of the ship, measured in kilometers per hour, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in hours. If the maximum cruising speed of the ship is $90$ $\text{km/h}$, which differential equation could be used to model the ship’s speed? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.worked_solution:
The rate at which the speed $V(t)$ of the ship changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum cruising speed and the current speed. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=k(a-V),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum cruising speed of the ship, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=90\text{ km/h},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=k(90-V).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Sinusoidal Forcing
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-9y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=A{e}^{3x}\,+\,($
{{field-1}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,+\,($
{{field-2}}
$)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
3\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}-9{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).$ So, we assume the particular solution to be 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-9(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(6\beta -9\alpha )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-6\alpha -9\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6\beta -9\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ -6\alpha -9\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{13},\beta =-\frac{6}{13}.$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{4}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{6}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+(-\frac{4}{13})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+(-\frac{6}{13})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Bernoulli Differential Equation to First Order Linear
questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=-\frac{x}{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-x,\,n=-1.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y,$ and we get

$$
y\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}=-x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z=-2x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-2x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Chain Rule for Differentiation
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we can write

$$
(f∘u)^{′}(t)={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now find the derivatives of each function.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(u) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡u) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}({e}^{u})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ {e}^{u}\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-3)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘u)^{′}(t) & ={f}^{′}(u(t)){u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u(t)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(u(t)) \\ {e}^{u(t)}\end{aligned}]\cdot {u}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t-3) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t-3) \\ {e}^{4t-3}\end{aligned}]\cdot 4 \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t-3) \\ -4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t-3) \\ 4{e}^{4t-3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$
- $⟨a,a⟩>0$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that if $a=0$ then $⟨a,a⟩=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
